measures_of_success: A larger share of scenario replies passes the model judge with the instructions than without, in both a chat setting and the deep-run prompt, with reference good replies passing and bad ones failing.
parameters: The evaluation model and judge model are chosen by environment settings; each arm is a function from a case to a reply. The instructions are a markdown file synced from the skill.
inputs: A scenario text with its expected behaviour and failure mode.
outputs: A reply, then a pass or fail verdict with a one-line reason from the judge.
effects: Real model calls that cost money, metered per run, with no repository change.
usage_notes: Run on a stratified subset with a call cap. Treat a lead inside the margin as a tie and prefer the arm that matches what actually ships.
selected_by: TIE, kept by the stated reason: the metric does not separate the standing instructions from the plain in-situ prompt (the pass rates are inside the leaderboard's margin for sampled, model-judged runs and the instructions spend more tokens), so the arm stays because quest_ai_runner/prompts/evolvable_structure.md is what the deep run actually loads (standing deep-run instructions, generated from the skill by scripts/sync_standing_instructions.py), and the arms without it are not what ships
gap: This is a tie, not a win: the recorded rows are stratified samples at the cheapest tier, and the same arms moved by several cases between two recordings on the same day, so a lead of a few cases is inside the noise and the leaderboard calls it a TIE. The judge and the replies are the same small model. The in-situ arm has no tools, so it scores the stated plan, not a diff from a real task. Calibration of the judge against Joshua's verdicts is pending his review of cases.csv.
action: Add Joshua's verdicts as labels when he has reviewed cases.csv in the sheet and re-calibrate the judge against them; score real deep-run diffs from actual tasks; run the full set once a stratified sample stops moving between recordings.

name: Behaviour-grading judge
scoped_purpose: Use for: grading whether a reply does what an evolvable-structure principle asks, by what it does rather than its vocabulary. Avoid: judging general quality, rewarding length or polish, and replacing a human reviewer.
goals: Raise agreement with the labelled reference replies, per side. Lower false passes and false fails. Keep cost to one cheap call per reply.
knowledge: Vocabulary alone can fool a check, so the model judge is told to grade what the reply does and extra polish earns nothing. A reply that states the exact edit counts even when no tools were available. The labels come from the case author who also wrote the regexes, so agreement shows the judge is not broken, not that it matches a human reading. An unparseable answer must count as a fail.
measures_of_success: Good reference replies pass and bad ones fail, with few false passes and false fails, over the behaviour cases.
parameters: The judge model is set by environment settings with a cheap default; the judge receives the case's expected behaviour and failure mode and a reply length cap.
inputs: A behaviour case (scenario, expected behaviour, failure mode) and a reply.
outputs: A verdict of pass or fail with a one-line reason.
effects: One model call per reply for the model judge, metered; none for the regex floor.
usage_notes: Use the model judge for scoring replies and keep the regex check only as a cheap prefilter. Recalibrate against human verdicts when they exist.
selected_by: evaluation/components/esoi_behavior/judge.py (build_judge), used by every judged esoi_behavior arm
gap: The labels come from the case author, who also wrote the regex checks, so agreement shows the judge is not broken, not that it matches Joshua's reading. Calibration against his verdicts is pending his review of cases.csv.
action: Add his verdicts as labels when he has reviewed the sheet and re-run; record the regex-only baseline arm beside it.

name: Public package surface contract
scoped_purpose: Use for: giving a consumer a package whose documented names import, whose registrations take effect, whose front doors build clients and configs from a clean environment, and whose shared helpers behave. Avoid: consumer-specific logic, network access at import time, and model calls.
goals: Make every documented name import. Make every registration and front door take effect on fixture inputs. Need no network or model to import.
knowledge: The package root is the one place that sees core, adapters and runner, so it wires what core needs without core importing them. Vendored editing code is kept because most of it absorbs specific ways real models get the format wrong, and an approximation would lose that quietly. A test shows a broken implementation that merely imports each name fails the cases.
measures_of_success: Public names, version, registrations, front-door outcomes, async bridge, signature probes, reply strippers, report builders, offline imports and vendored edit cases all pass.
parameters: Front doors take an optional config file path and a timeout; the async bridge takes a coroutine or a blocking function with arguments. No other tuning exists.
inputs: A config path or environment for the front doors; coroutines or callables for the bridge; text for the edit parser.
outputs: A configured client or runner config, results of bridged calls, parsed edit blocks and applied edits.
effects: The package root installs core wiring at import; the bridge starts one long-lived background loop; nothing opens a network connection at import.
usage_notes: Import from the package root and use the front doors rather than re-deriving environment variable names. Add a case whenever a new name enters the docs.
area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
selected_by: quest_ai_runner/__init__.py (the package root, load_config, load_client), core/async_bridge.py, core/signature_probe.py, core/scaffolding.py, bootstrap_email.py, vendor/
invariant_reason: A documented name imports or it does not; the public surface is a promise to consumers.
gap: The name list is hand-written from the docs, so a new public name is covered only once someone adds a case. A broken implementation that only imports each name is shown by a test to fail the cases, because names and imports are the easy part.
action: Add a case when a name enters the README or docs/writing-a-consumer.md.

name: Runnable example set
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a newcomer learn the library from small examples that still compile, import, run their offline path, are introduced in the examples index, and leak nothing. Avoid: examples needing live services in this check, and teaching by prose alone.
goals: Keep every example runnable on an empty environment. Keep each introduced in the index. Keep secrets and machine paths out.
knowledge: Three consumers once each hand-wrote the same lane driver, so the minimal example shows how little a lane must supply once the shared driver and config exist. Examples read everything from the environment with placeholders. Demos that need a live backend or a terminal can only be scored on import, refusal to start and stub behaviour.
measures_of_success: Each example compiles, imports, reaches its help or not-configured exit in a scrubbed environment, appears in the index, and passes the secret and path scan.
parameters: Each example takes its own command-line modes (check, once, loop) and reads configuration from a file layered under environment variables, with the environment winning.
inputs: A config file and environment variables; no secrets are baked in.
outputs: A running lane or a built runner configuration, and help or not-configured messages on an empty environment.
effects: The lane example may poll a backend when configured; offline paths have none.
usage_notes: Copy the minimal lane to start, adapt the custom consumer for a specific organisation, and add a file to the index in the same change.
selected_by: examples/ as shipped (README.md lists each file)
invariant_reason: An example runs as documented on an empty environment or it does not.
gap: e2e_demo.py and textual_demo.py need a live Quest backend and a terminal, so only their import, refusal-to-start and stub behaviour are scored, not a full run.
action: None for the offline arm; a live arm belongs with the dev-Quest world in evaluation/qualitative.

name: Queued-task runner lane
scoped_purpose: Use for: taking a task someone queued for the assistant to a reported outcome, claimed once, run by the right persona, and reported done, failed or needing the person. Avoid: running a task twice, dropping it, running it before its time, and deciding what the task should be.
goals: Claim each due task once. Run it as the right persona against its work folder. Report an outcome for every task. Run none early.
knowledge: Discovery is event driven with signature dedup across restarts and a backend-aware claim as a second guard. A persona activates only when asked for, never from a bare mention of a name. Folder sync keeps human text and pushes each bullet once. Cancelled tasks need no patch because the backend already set the status.
measures_of_success: Poll, claim, run and report behave correctly across done, failed, needs-you, duplicate, lost-claim, not-yet-due, team-scoped and unconfigured cases, with persona choice, folder sync and scheduling correct.
parameters: The poller takes a configuration with credentials, team, adapters and a concurrency bound; personas take a skills root, registry, assignment fields and flags for model-judged asks; the lane driver takes check, once or loop modes and an env file.
inputs: Queued tasks from the backend, the configuration, persona registry and folder map.
outputs: A reported status on each task (with result text or decision id), updated folder sync files, and logs.
effects: Claims tasks on the backend, writes the sync file in work folders, may post notes, and spawns deep runs.
usage_notes: Start a lane with the shared driver and pick one-shot mode for cron or loop mode for a service. Use structured assignment for personas where tasks name an owner.
selected_by: runner/config_wiring.py (a lane's run_lane drives Poller and TaskExecutor)
invariant_reason: A due task is claimed once and reported, or one is lost or duplicated; the lifecycle is a contract.
gap: The edge is a fake Quest client and a scripted model, so wire-level behaviour (HTTP errors, real Quest payload shapes) is not scored here; those are pinned by the quest_client tests and the dev-Quest qualitative run.
action: Add crash-recovery (orphaned in-flight claims) and provider-outage requeue cases when those paths next change.

name: Layered lane configuration loader
scoped_purpose: Use for: turning a configuration file plus environment variables into one validated runner configuration at startup, with a defined precedence between sources. Avoid: wiring adapters from the resulting configuration, and per-request or per-turn overrides.
goals: Maximise correct precedence across file, environment and process sources; maximise the share of typos, unsupported keys and malformed values that are rejected or defaulted as specified; keep model calls at zero.
knowledge: A lane is operated by people who edit a file and export variables, so a silent typo or a surprising winner between sources costs a deployment. Past design lessons: the file is a baseline, the core package must never read the process environment directly, and tuning values must tolerate bad input by falling back to defaults so a running process can be retuned without a restart.
measures_of_success: Every precedence rule holds in every probed combination, every invalid key is refused loudly before the lane starts, and a bad tuning value never stops the lane.
parameters: A path to a TOML file (or none), plus the set of file-expressible fields owned by the configuration dataclass; tuning values are read from an optional environment mapping.
inputs: The configuration file text, additional environment files it references, the process environment, and the environment tables inside the file.
outputs: A populated runner configuration object, or a configuration-file error naming the offending key; tuning values come back as one typed settings value.
effects: Exports file-defined environment values into the process environment where the precedence rules allow, and installs the tuning-settings provider used by the core package.
usage_notes: Call at startup, before building any adapter; use the file for baselines and environment variables for per-deployment overrides. Add a file-expressible field only together with its precedence or validation rule.
invariant_reason: Precedence and the loud rejection of a typo are rules the configuration follows or breaks.
gap: Covers the scalar fields a lane commonly sets, not every one of the roughly 100 RunnerConfig fields; adapter wiring from the resulting config is covered by the run_queued_tasks and route_a_message components.
action: Add a case per new file-expressible field only when it carries precedence or validation logic of its own.

name: Non-interactive command-line surface
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a person or a deep run's shell invoke the runner and its tool catalog through subcommands with stable parsing, output and exit codes. Avoid: the interactive chat terminal, the poll loop, the channel and file-serving surfaces, which need a terminal or a server.
goals: Maximise the share of subcommands that parse and print what a person needs to act; maximise bad invocations refused with the usage exit code before any action; keep model calls at zero.
knowledge: A deep run reaches the same tools through a shell, so the command line is a fixed contract that other processes depend on. Design lessons: write-capable methods must be refused unless explicitly allowed, maintenance commands default to a dry run, and missing credentials must produce a message that says what to set.
measures_of_success: Every subcommand answers help, unknown commands and flags and malformed arguments are refused with the usage code, write methods are refused without the write flag, and the tool catalog lists, shows and calls tools correctly.
parameters: A subcommand with its flags; the quest command takes a method name and keyword pairs, the context commands take store locations and an apply flag, the tool entry point takes list, show or call with keyword or JSON arguments.
inputs: The argument vector, the process environment for credentials, and files or a store folder the command points at.
outputs: Text on standard output and error and an integer exit code, with zero for success and the usage code for a refused invocation.
effects: Write subcommands change Quest data or card stores only when explicitly allowed; context maintenance commands are dry runs unless an apply flag is given.
usage_notes: Use from scripts and from a deep run's shell; prefer the read-only form first, add the write or apply flag deliberately, and add a case when a subcommand or flag is added.
area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
selected_by: pyproject console script quest-ai-runner and python -m quest_ai_runner.tools
invariant_reason: A subcommand parses and prints what it should or it does not; the command line is a fixed surface.
gap: The interactive surfaces (chat TUI, poll loop, channel, serve-files) need a terminal or a server and are pinned only by their own tests, not scored here.
action: Drive the chat UI through Textual's pilot in a future arm if a regression slips past the unit tests.

name: Cost-ordered model tier selector with outage and allowance recovery
scoped_purpose: Use for: choosing which model rung starts a piece of work, resolving a family or tier name to the newest live release, falling back when a tier is exhausted, and recognising provider outages and usage limits so work resumes later. Avoid: judging whether the cheapest model still succeeded, which needs live runs, and the routing of a message itself.
goals: Maximise the share of work started on the cheapest adequate rung; maximise correct resolution of names to live models with operator pins always winning; maximise correct recognition of outages and allowance limits and of their reset time.
knowledge: The planner already rates difficulty on the call that decides the route, so starting-model choice costs no extra model call. Past incidents: queued tasks failed outright when a provider briefly overloaded and had to be rerun by hand, and a subscription allowance limit looks like a failed run rather than an outage, so each needs its own recognition and a resume time.
measures_of_success: Each difficulty maps to the stated starting rung, family names track new releases without edits, a pin always wins, an exhausted tier falls to the next cheaper one, and outages and limits are recognised with a correct resume time.
parameters: A difficulty rating, a ladder of rungs, optional operator model mapping and pins, a tier or family name, the list of live models, and the current time for limit parsing.
inputs: The planner's difficulty rating, a provider's live model list, error or result text from a failed model call, and the clock.
outputs: A starting model and ladder, a concrete model id for a tier or family, the next lower tier, a vision-capability answer, an outage verdict, and a usage-limit record with its reset and resume times.
effects: Remembers the latest outage and usage limit lane-wide, optionally persisted to a file, so other tasks hold off until the resume time.
usage_notes: Resolve names through the registry at the point of use rather than pinning release ids; set an operator pin only when a specific model is required. Treat an outage as a reason to requeue, not to fail the task.
invariant_reason: The tier chosen follows stated rules (difficulty to starting rung, an operator pin wins, an exhausted tier falls to the next cheaper one); each rule holds or it does not.
gap: Measures that the right model is chosen, not that the choice was the cheapest one that still succeeded; that needs live runs (route_a_message and the qualitative eval).
action: Record a cost-per-success arm once a live model spend is approved.

name: Cost estimation, daily budget and host load guard
scoped_purpose: Use for: estimating what an operation will cost before it spends, stopping new work at a daily token budget, and pausing pickup when the host is overloaded. Avoid: output-token billing, real provider invoices, and work done by a subscription-based deep runner, which does not count toward the budget.
goals: Maximise correctness of per-model price lookup with a stated default for unknown models; maximise budget accuracy across restarts and day boundaries; minimise flapping of the host guard by using hysteresis.
knowledge: Shallow orchestrator calls can run away on cost, so a daily cap is opt-in and persisted. Pausing pickup is lossless because unclaimed tasks stay queued and fire on a later scan. Prices are a hand-kept snapshot of list prices, so a provider change is not noticed until the table is edited.
measures_of_success: Prices and estimates are arithmetically right, the daily total survives a restart and resets each day, bad or negative values are handled, and the guard pauses and resumes without flapping.
parameters: Provider and model names, a token count, daily limit and usage path from the environment, and optional host limits for memory percent, free memory and load.
inputs: Token counts per call, environment variables, and host samples of memory and load.
outputs: A price per million input tokens, a bootstrap cost estimate with the provider and model used, a running total with an over-limit flag and status line, and a paused or not verdict.
effects: Writes the day's tally to a usage file and signals the poller to stop picking up new tasks while over budget or overloaded; in-flight tasks are never killed.
usage_notes: Both limits are opt-in; set them per lane. Review the price table whenever a provider changes prices.
selected_by: runner/poller.py (ResourceGuard, DailyUsageTracker) and cli_context bootstrap estimate
invariant_reason: Prices, budgets and guard thresholds are arithmetic that is right or wrong.
gap: Prices are a hand-kept snapshot of list prices (input tokens only), so a provider price change is not noticed until the table is edited.
action: Review the price table whenever a provider announces a change; add output-token pricing if cost reporting needs it.

selected_by: CLAUDE.md pre-commit rule: run only the tests your change touches; this collection check is the cheap whole-suite gate
invariant_reason: Every test file collects and none disappears, or the suite is broken; collection has no better and worse.

name: Public-repository hygiene scanner
scoped_purpose: Use for: finding secrets, real machine paths, object ids and real addresses in working files before they are committed to a public repository. Avoid: scanning git history, and detecting a secret shape the scanner has no pattern for.
goals: Maximise detection of every known secret kind planted in text; minimise false findings on documented placeholders; keep the repository itself scanning clean.
knowledge: A public repository must hold nothing consumer specific or secret, and documentation needs to show the shape of a secret without being flagged, so placeholders are explicitly allowed. A secret already committed must be rotated, since the scan does not read history. Findings print a redacted snippet, never the whole secret.
measures_of_success: Every planted secret kind is found, every documented placeholder stays quiet, the repository scans clean, and the command exits with failure on any finding.
parameters: A repository root, an option to scan only staged files, and optional file selection.
inputs: Text or files known to git (tracked, or untracked and not ignored).
outputs: A list of findings with a pattern name, a location and a redacted snippet, and an exit code that is nonzero on any finding.
effects: None; it reads files only and changes nothing.
usage_notes: Run before every commit, including staged-only mode in a commit step. Add a pattern and a planted test case together whenever a new credential shape appears.
area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
invariant_reason: A planted secret is found or it is not; the scan is a rule with no quality dial.
gap: The scan reads working files unless `esoi hygiene --history` is asked for, and knows only the secret shapes in the esoi hygiene scanner: a vendor token with a new shape passes until the scanner gains a pattern and a planted case is added here.

name: Documentation coverage and voice check
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a newcomer or an AI learn the runner from its documents, by checking links, index reachability, coverage of variables, subcommands and public names, and house voice. Avoid: judging whether the prose is clear or correct, and checking examples by running them.
goals: Minimise broken links and orphan documents; maximise coverage of every environment variable, subcommand and public name; eliminate disallowed punctuation from documents.

measures_of_success: Every generated documentation case passes: no broken link, no document unreachable from the index, nothing undocumented, no em dash.
parameters: The documents folder, an index file, a generated configuration reference, and the generator that produces cases.
inputs: The markdown files, the package's public names and the real argument tree.
outputs: Pass or fail per case, naming the broken link, missing description or offending document.
effects: None; documents are read only.
usage_notes: Update the index when adding a document, document each new variable and subcommand, and regenerate cases rather than hand-editing them.
area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
invariant_reason: Every link, document, variable and name is covered or it is not; documentation coverage is checked rule by rule.
gap: Some documents still contain em dashes, against the house voice rule; the failing cases name each one.

name: Scoped prediction store
scoped_purpose: Use for: keeping what an anticipation engine learned (recurring-ask patterns, live predictions with precomputed views, an outcome log) per scope across turns and restarts. Avoid: judging whether predictions are right, which is not measured here, and cross-scope sharing.
goals: Maximise exact round trip of saved data; maximise scope isolation; maximise correct expiry; maximise survival across a restart; ensure no store call raises.
knowledge: The store sits behind a port so a consumer with its own database can supply one. Storage must be best-effort and never raise into a turn. Prediction quality is a separate unmeasured question: the engine logs each prediction against the actual next message, but no replayed corpus scores it.
measures_of_success: A store passes every contract scenario: round trip, isolation, replace, expiry, view, clear, log, restart and tolerance.
parameters: A scope key per call, patterns, predictions with an expiry time and optional views, and a log record.
inputs: Pattern and prediction records and the scope key.
outputs: The saved patterns, the unexpired predictions, a precomputed view text by prediction id, or nothing for a write.
effects: Writes persistent state (a file per scope and an outcome log in the file store) and drops expired predictions on load.
usage_notes: Implement the port's methods to add a backend and run the same contract scenarios against it; choose the file store for a lane, an in-memory store only as a reference.
invariant_reason: A store returns exactly what was saved, per scope, or it breaks the contract; backends differ in where data lives, not in how well they store it.
gap: The in-memory reference fails the restart scenario by design; a consumer-side database store (quest-backend) is not scored here. Prediction quality is not measured at all: this contract says whether a store keeps what it was given, not whether the anticipation engine predicts the next ask. The engine logs every prediction against the actual next message, but no case set replays recorded ask sequences through it, so nothing says how often a served prediction is right or what a wrong one costs

Build a replay metric for the anticipation engine (recorded ask sequences with known next asks, scored by the share of served predictions that match and the extra cost of a miss) as its own solution once a corpus exists

name: Autopilot run-or-skip gate
scoped_purpose: Use for: deciding per quest, before any goal is read or model called, whether a recurring autopilot pass should work now, according to the person's settings. Avoid: judging what a pass does once it runs, and whether the moment suits the person.
goals: Maximise correct run and skip decisions against the person's settings; eliminate runs past the daily budget or on a day nobody was rostered; minimise spend before the decision.
knowledge: A wrong run spends and sends against the person's setting, and a wrong skip loses a day, so the gate is a rule, not a quality dial. Cadence is judged in the quest's own time zone with a roster of days, not by elapsed time, and a pending Run now request or a reactive trigger can override cadence. Backpressure also holds a quest.
measures_of_success: Every labelled gate case ends as skipped for the right reason or as past every gate, and a baseline that uses elapsed-time cadence with no roster fails the cases.
parameters: A daily budget, a backpressure flag, a clock, and per-quest autopilot settings (cadence, Run now, reactive trigger, roster days).
inputs: The quest list, each quest's autopilot settings, open tasks and asks, open decisions, and the current time.
outputs: For each quest, either a skip with a reason or passage through every gate to the work stage.
effects: Counts against the daily budget when a quest is worked; before the gates pass, no goals are read and no model is called.
usage_notes: Place every eligibility rule in the gate, before any expensive read, and add a case for each new rule or setting.
selected_by: runner/autopilot_gates.py GatesMixin._gate_quest, the budget check in AutopilotPass.run and the pure predicates in runner/autopilot_periods.py
invariant_reason: The person's settings (daily budget, cadence, Run now, reactive trigger, roster days) are rules the gate follows or breaks; a gate that runs a quest on a day nobody was rostered is wrong, not merely worse.
gap: Only the decision to run is scored. What a pass writes once it runs (the brief, the goals it proposes, the persona work) is measured for size by assemble-a-prompt and is otherwise unmeasured, and whether the moment suits the person is not scored, only that their settings are followed.
action: Add pass-output cases (the work items a pass creates from a quest state) when real passes can be shared without private data.
